newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank chalks up victory over Bonn on gold row.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank chalks up victory over Bonn on gold row.

text.p: The Bundesbank on Tuesday scored a strategic victory over Bonn after holding talks to end a bitter gold row, signaling that it would not turn into a lame-duck central bank during the last days before currency union.

"The Bundesbank is clearly the one that has come out on top of this," said Ros Lifton, economist at HSBC Markets in London, of an eleventh-hour solution to the most public controversy waged between Bonn and the Frankfurt-based Bundesbank in years.

At issue was Finance Minister Theo Waigel's hastily unveiled plan to revalue German assets and receive a portion of the unrealised profits this year to help pave over his gaping budget holes and help squeeze Germany into EMU on time.
Currency union is scheduled to begin with those nations meeting strict fiscal entry targets on January 1, 1999.

The Bundesbank sternly rebuffed Waigel's plans, arguing it would harm currency union if Germany, the driving force for a strong common currency, all of a sudden indulged in the creative accounting tricks it had scolded others for using.

Although both sides appeared to have made concessions, Waigel by agreeing to receive no extra money from any revaluation this year, and the Bundesbank by agreeing to a revaluation before EMU begins, many analysts said Bonn emerged more bruised.

"Effectively, the Finance Ministry lost credibility for no extra gain," said Francis Breedon, economist at Lehman Brothers in London, noting Waigel still faces the same budget problems he did before stumbling into this public relations debacle.
Thomas Mayer, economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt, added "the compromise does not solve Waigel's problems, he is still looking for extra money."

Even though the Bundesbank also gave up some ground by agreeing to a payout next year, analysts stressed the central bank won by effectively forcing Bonn to stick to its own moral high ground on the EMU issue.

Should Bonn have received the green light for a transfer of funds and used these to pare back debt and the deficit, Germany would have been just as guilty of tinkering with the Maastricht Treaty criteria as other nations are, analysts said.

"The Bundesbank is not happy that this happened at all, but if the revaluation is handled prudently and it is not linked to 1997 accounts and cannot be called a fudge, then they have done their bit," said HSBC's Lifton.

Economists were split in opinion over the long-term effect on Germany's own credibility however in the wake of an issue that arounsed the public and left the Finance Minister even more beleaguered than before.

Sitting across from a new French government which has said it wishes to renegotiate the stability pact and wishes to increase a stability council's powers, Germany will have to fight hard to launch a small currency union that would exclude some countries.
"Germany once had a very powerful stick to force its demands on its partners, but that is gone now," Lifton said.

As Waigel scrambles to find new cost cutting measures or lobbies coalition partners to agree to a tax hike, economists said it might be wiser for Germany to back off its hardline reading on EMU goals. But this too could be seen as a policy U-turn, they added.
Analysts also agreed that the Bundesbank's careful manouevering during these wranglings made clear that Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer is the better strategist.
Cleverly playing its hand and uniting public opinion behind it, the Bundesbank showed Bonn it is clearly capable of standing up for its opinions.

"This could be seen as a warning to Bonn," Lifton said, adding "this was just the first battle and it shows what could happen when it comes time to discuss the possible participants in currency union next spring."
While clearly not turning into a lame-duck central bank, economists also warned the Bundesbank would not breach its mandate, firing back only if the ball lands in its court.
"The ball would be in the Bundesbank's court on rates, or France's plan to alter the stability pact or set up a stronger stability council," said Goldman's Mayer.

For the markets, the first reading on the compromise was positive and economists added a realisation that the Bundesbank is still very much in charge of German monetary policy would also be a supportive factor.
